newsitem.title: USA: Highlights of the landmark tobacco settlement.
newsitem.headline: Highlights of the landmark tobacco settlement.

text.p: The following are highlights of the tentative agreement reached Friday between state negotiators and the tobacco industry, according to a statement issued by the state attorneys general:

-- The tobacco industry pays $368.5 billion over 25 years into a fund from which personal injury claims would be paid and health care programmes funded. Of this, about $308 billion will be to settle lawsuits and $60 billion for punitive damages. The annual payments by the industry would be adjusted for inflation by 3 percent annually.

-- The total amount the industry would have to pay through litigation in any one year would be capped at $5 billion, according to the National Centre for Tobacco-Free Kids, which represented health groups in the negotiations.
-- The tobacco industry would formally recognise that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has regulatory power over tobacco products and could eventually ban nicotine.

"After 12 years, the agency will be authorised to eliminate nicotine entirely, but to do so in a manner that gives Congress time to review, if it so desires," said a statement by the National Centre for Tobacco-Free Kids.
The health group also said the industry agreed to drop its legal challenge to the FDA's right to regulate tobacco.

-- Cigarette makers agree to sharp restrictions on advertising that would appeal to children. This would include elimination of all cartoon characters and human images from cigarette packages. It would also ban billboard and outdoor signs, including signs in stadiums and arenas.
-- Industry agrees to funding for nationwide public anti-smoking education programme.

-- Industry agrees to dramatic revision of the warning labels on cigarette packages. This would include moving the label to the front of the package. The warning would occupy 25 percent of the front of the package. The labels would include new language that would say that cigarettes are addictive and that tobacco smoke causes fatal lung disease in non-smokers.
-- The industry would be subject to penalties if underage smoking fails to drop by 42 percent in five years, 58 percent in seven years and 67 percent in 10 years.
-- The industry agrees to pay for programmes to help people give up smoking and for anti-smoking devices for people who can not afford to pay for them.

-- The industry agrees to protect so-called whistle-blowers, or employees of cigarette companies who provide evidence against their employers. That contentious issue was one of the final sticking points in the negotiations.

-- President Bill Clinton names two top administration officials, Health and Human Services Secretary Donnal Shalala and White House aide Bruce Reed, to head panel to review agreement to insure it protects the public health.
